concept_edges.logic: x = y stores the value of y in x (a statement with a side effect); x == y only tests whether the two values are equal and gives a boolean. Writing = where == is meant is a compile error with int operands and a silent bug with boolean operands.
An if runs its block only when its boolean expression evaluates to true.
A comparison such as x < y produces a boolean result; comparisons together with boolean logic provide the basis for decision-making.
An if changes the default top-to-bottom flow by running a block only when its condition is true.
Comparison operators build expressions whose value is a boolean, so one must already know what an expression is to understand a < b.
Control flow is the order in which statements run.
System.out.println(s); is itself a statement, so its line of output appears at its own place in the sequence.
println("s") outputs exactly the characters between the quotes and then ends the line.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A true/false question is answered with arithmetic (e.g. 1 for true).
misconceptions.correct_rule: A logic question is written as a boolean expression whose value is true or false.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: = compares two values instead of assigning
misconceptions.correct_rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Assigns a new value to a variable declared final.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A final variable cannot be reassigned after it is initialized; the compiler reports an error.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a = b adds the value of b to the value already in a (the accumulator model).
misconceptions.correct_rule: a = b replaces the old value of a with the value of b; the old value is lost.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: assigning a reference copies the object
misconceptions.correct_rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: After b = a, a no longer holds a value, as if the value had been moved.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Assignment copies; the variable on the right keeps its value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: b = a exchanges the values of a and b.
misconceptions.correct_rule: b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities.
misconceptions.correct_rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression
misconceptions.correct_rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a = b copies the value of a into b.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Indenting several statements under an if or for makes them all part of its body, even without braces.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Without braces only the first statement belongs to the if/for; the rest run once, after it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Which branch runs is decided by what the programmer meant or by code outside the if, not by whether the condition is true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The then branch runs exactly when the condition evaluates to true at the moment it is tested; otherwise the else branch (if any) runs.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: 90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100.
misconceptions.correct_rule: a < b < c does not compile (a < b is a boolean); a range test is written 90 <= grade && grade <= 100.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped.
misconceptions.correct_rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: you must write == true / == false to test a boolean
misconceptions.correct_rule: if (b) already tests b, so writing == true adds nothing.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The computer executes only what the code states; every needed step and value must be written.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes the if condition inside { } instead of ( ).
misconceptions.correct_rule: The condition of an if is written in parentheses.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes else (x > 0) with a condition but no if.
misconceptions.correct_rule: else takes no condition; use else if (x > 0).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: == compares contents (the String == bug)
misconceptions.correct_rule: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; s.equals(t) compares the text.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: .equals() compares references, not contents
misconceptions.correct_rule: s.equals(t) checks whether the two Strings contain the same characters.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes a + b = c; or 7 = a; as if = were a math equation.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The left side of an assignment must be a single variable; only the right side can be an expression.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A false condition with no else ends the program.
misconceptions.correct_rule: When an if condition is false and there is no else, execution continues with the statement after the if.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Whether the branch runs is decided by the condition after the branch, or from the point inside the body where the condition becomes true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The condition is tested once, before the branch; the whole branch runs if it was true at that moment and none of it runs otherwise.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever).
misconceptions.correct_rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An if inside a loop body runs its branch on every pass without testing its condition.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The if condition is tested again on every pass, with the current values, so the branch runs only on passes where it is true.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: an if body repeats while its condition holds
misconceptions.correct_rule: An if body runs at most once; only a loop repeats its body.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Every if statement requires an else.
misconceptions.correct_rule: An if statement may stand alone; the else part is optional.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: < and > mean the same thing (or a < b means a is greater than b).
misconceptions.correct_rule: a < b is true when a is smaller than b; a > b when a is larger.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Uses a loop where a condition needs to be tested only once.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A test made once is an if; a loop repeats.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: you need ? : to do the same
misconceptions.correct_rule: ok = (x > y); already gives the boolean, so the ? : is unnecessary.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: you need an if to turn a boolean expression into a boolean
misconceptions.correct_rule: ok = (x > y); stores the result of the comparison directly.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Omits braces around a single-statement body of if, for or while.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Braces are optional for a single-statement body, but using them anyway avoids bugs when statements are added later.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A condition on several values has to be written as nested if statements, one value per if.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Several conditions combine into one boolean expression with && and ||, e.g. if (x == 0 && y == 0).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: In if (c) A; B; the statement B runs only when c is false.
misconceptions.correct_rule: B is not part of the if; it runs every time.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a single literal or variable "isn't an expression"
misconceptions.correct_rule: A single variable or literal is an expression whose value is just that value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: logical AND/OR always evaluate both sides (Java short-circuits them)
misconceptions.correct_rule: In p && q, q is evaluated only when p is true; in p || q, q is evaluated only when p is false.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: nested calls run outside-in, not arguments-first
misconceptions.correct_rule: In f(g(x)), g(x) is evaluated first and its result is passed to f.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: () are optional on a no-argument call like println
misconceptions.correct_rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: print and println behave the same (no newline difference)
misconceptions.correct_rule: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: println(s) prints a newline and then s.
misconceptions.correct_rule: println(s) prints s and then the newline.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Ends the output with print and expects it to appear right away.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Finish a line of print calls with println; some systems hold print output until a newline is printed.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.println("x is 5"); sets x to 5 (text inside the quotes is run as code).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Characters inside double quotes are printed literally; println only displays them and changes no variable. Only an assignment such as x = 5; sets x.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs.
misconceptions.correct_rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes int x = 5; ... int x = 10; to change x.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A declaration gives a variable its name and type; a later change of value is an assignment statement such as x = 10;, not a second declaration.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A return inside a loop does not end the loop; it sets a value each pass (the last one is returned) or returns several values.
misconceptions.correct_rule: When return executes, the method ends at once, so the loop stops on that pass.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes =< or => instead of <= and >=.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The operators are written <= and >=.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: if (x > 0); System.out.println("positive"); prints only for positive x.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The ; ends the if with an empty statement, so the next line always runs.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Of two if statements one after the other, the second runs its body only if both conditions are true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Two ifs in sequence are independent: each tests only its own condition.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes a string literal in single quotes: 'Hello'.
misconceptions.correct_rule: String literals use double quotes; single quotes are for one char.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A statement placed after the if statement belongs to its branch, so it runs only when the condition is true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The branch ends at its closing brace (or after its single statement); the next statement runs whatever the condition was.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a statement runs without the ;
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each statement must end with ;, otherwise javac reports ';' expected.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Statements in a program can run in any order.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Breaks a string literal across two lines of code.
misconceptions.correct_rule: String literals must not span more than one line of a program.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: s < t compares two Strings alphabetically.
misconceptions.correct_rule: < and > are defined only for primitive types; comparing Strings with them does not compile.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The type of a numerical expression depends on the type expected by the surrounding context, so double d = a / b; keeps the fraction.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The type of a numerical expression is determined by the expression, so double d = a / b; with int a and b still divides as ints.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The then branch always runs.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The then branch runs only when the condition is true.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A string literal can be left without its closing quote.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A String literal is enclosed in a pair of double quotes.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value
misconceptions.correct_rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java compilers consider all whitespace in program text (outside quotation marks) to be equivalent; layout is for human readers.

level_mis_links.exact_rule: wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
wrong rule: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression. Right rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.
wrong rule: a = b copies the value of a into b. Right rule: Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.
wrong rule: a = b adds the value of b to the value already in a (the accumulator model). Right rule: a = b replaces the old value of a with the value of b; the old value is lost.

wrong rule: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities. Right rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.
wrong rule: b = a exchanges the values of a and b. Right rule: b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.
wrong rule: After b = a, a no longer holds a value, as if the value had been moved. Right rule: Assignment copies; the variable on the right keeps its value.

Points to LT (evaluate the right side with current values, then overwrite the left variable). Applied unevenly, a student traces one segment correctly but reads the next as simultaneous equations or as a swap, giving 15 and 15 for one segment and 5 and 10 for the other. (here mixing in: "= stores the expression itself, not its computed value")
wrong rule: a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values. Right rule: A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.
wrong rule: assigning a reference copies the object. Right rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].
wrong rule: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model). Right rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

Swapping the two sides (a = b versus b = a) changes which variable changes. Reordering assignments changes the final values. An assignment cannot be undone, because the old value is lost unless it was first saved in a temporary.
wrong rule: You must write == true / == false to test a boolean. Right rule: if (b) already tests b, and if (!b) tests that it is false, so == true adds nothing.
wrong rule: You need an if to turn a boolean expression into a boolean. Right rule: ok = (x > y); stores the result of the comparison directly.
wrong rule: You need ? : to turn a boolean expression into a boolean (ok = x > y ? true : false). Right rule: ok = (x > y); already gives the boolean, so the ? : is unnecessary.
wrong rule: A true/false question is answered with arithmetic (e.g. 1 for true). Right rule: A logic question is written as a boolean expression whose value is true or false, e.g. (year % 4 == 0).

Points to LT (arithmetic first, then comparisons, then !, &&, ||, left to right, with short-circuit). Applied unevenly: the student evaluates && before a comparison in one sub-expression, or evaluates the right operand of && on a pass where the left was already false. (here mixing in: "you must write == true / == false to test a boolean")

wrong rule: 90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100. Right rule: a < b < c does not compile (a < b is a boolean, which cannot be compared with <); a range test is written 90 <= grade && grade <= 100.

wrong rule: Uses a loop where a condition needs to be tested only once. Right rule: A test made once is an if; a while re-tests its condition and repeats its body for as long as the condition is true.

wrong rule: A condition on several values has to be written as nested if statements, one value per if. Right rule: Several conditions combine into one boolean expression with && and ||, e.g. if (x == 0 && y == 0).

Rewriting with De Morgan (!(a && b) as !a || !b) keeps the value for every input; swapping the operands of && keeps the truth value but can change whether the right operand is evaluated (and whether a guard still protects it); changing < to <= changes the result only at the boundary value.
wrong rule: 90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100. Right rule: a < b < c does not compile (a < b is a boolean); a range test is written 90 <= grade && grade <= 100.

wrong rule: == compares the contents of two Strings. Right rule: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; "abc" == "ab" + x is false even when x is "c"; s.equals(t) compares the text.
wrong rule: s < t compares two Strings alphabetically. Right rule: < and > are defined only for primitive types; comparing Strings with them does not compile (use s.compareTo(t)).
wrong rule: < and > mean the same thing (or a < b means a is greater than b). Right rule: a < b is true when a is smaller than b; a > b when a is larger.

Points to LT (evaluate both operands, promote to a common type, then compare). Applied unevenly: the student treats < as <= on the boundary pass of a loop, or compares an int with a double as ints on one line and as doubles on another. (here mixing in: "90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100")
wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them and produces a boolean.
wrong rule: You must write == true / == false to test a boolean. Right rule: if (b) already tests b, so writing == true adds nothing.
wrong rule: .equals() compares references, not contents. Right rule: s.equals(t) checks whether the two Strings contain the same characters; it is == that compares references.

Changing < to <= (or > to >=) changes the result only at the boundary value, which in a loop guard means one more or one fewer iteration (off-by-one); mirroring the comparison (a < b to b > a) preserves the value; negating it gives the complementary operator (!(a < b) is a >= b).
wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order. Right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom.

wrong rule: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.

Applies the sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: e.g. runs a later line before an earlier one, lets an if that was already passed fire again later, or ends the program when a loop or a false if ends instead of continuing with the next statement. (here mixing in: "Statements in a program can run in any order")
wrong rule: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped. Right rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way.
wrong rule: logical AND/OR always evaluate both sides (Java short-circuits them). Right rule: In p && q, q is evaluated only when p is true; in p || q, q is evaluated only when p is false.

wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. Right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop.

wrong rule: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true. Right rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it.

wrong rule: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program. Right rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement.

wrong rule: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever). Right rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch.
wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. Right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop.

wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. Right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.

Reordering two statements generally changes the result whenever one reads a variable that the other writes (e.g. swapping x = x + 1 and print(x)); reordering is safe only for statements that touch disjoint variables. Moving a statement into or out of a branch or loop body changes how many times it runs (0, 1 or n).
wrong rule: a single literal or variable "isn't an expression". Right rule: A single variable or literal is an expression whose value is just that value.

Points to LT (replace each variable with its current value, then apply operators in precedence order). Applied unevenly, a student substitutes current values for some variables and old or future values for others, or respects precedence in one subexpression only. (here mixing in: "a single literal or variable "isn't an expression"")
wrong rule: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression. Right rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.
wrong rule: () are optional on a no-argument call like println. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

wrong rule: The type of a numerical expression depends on the type expected by the surrounding context, so double d = a / b; keeps the fraction. Right rule: The type of a numerical expression is determined by the expression, so double d = a / b; with int a and b still divides as ints.
wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
wrong rule: nested calls run outside-in, not arguments-first. Right rule: In f(g(x)), g(x) is evaluated first and its result is passed to f.

wrong rule: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities. Right rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.

Adding parentheses that match the default grouping keeps the value, and rewriting with an equivalent formula (4 * (x - 3) as 4*x - 12) keeps it for ints. Changing one operand's type (3 to 3.0) can change both the result's type and its value.
wrong rule: an if body repeats while its condition holds. Right rule: An if body runs at most once; only a loop repeats its body.
wrong rule: Every if statement requires an else. Right rule: An if statement may stand alone; the else part is optional.
wrong rule: A false condition with no else ends the program. Right rule: When an if condition is false and there is no else, execution continues with the statement after the if.
wrong rule: The then branch always runs. Right rule: The then branch runs only when the condition is true.
wrong rule: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped. Right rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way.
wrong rule: In if (c) A; B; the statement B runs only when c is false. Right rule: B is not part of the if; it runs every time.

wrong rule: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true. Right rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it.

wrong rule: Which branch runs is decided by what the programmer meant or by code outside the if, not by whether the condition is true. Right rule: The then branch runs exactly when the condition evaluates to true at the moment it is tested; otherwise the else branch (if any) runs.

wrong rule: A statement placed after the if statement belongs to its branch, so it runs only when the condition is true. Right rule: The branch ends at its closing brace (or after its single statement); the next statement runs whatever the condition was.

wrong rule: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program. Right rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement.

wrong rule: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever). Right rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch.

wrong rule: Whether the branch runs is decided by the condition after the branch, or from the point inside the body where the condition becomes true. Right rule: The condition is tested once, before the branch; the whole branch runs if it was true at that moment and none of it runs otherwise.

wrong rule: An if inside a loop body runs its branch on every pass without testing its condition. Right rule: The if condition is tested again on every pass, with the current values, so the branch runs only on passes where it is true.

Applies the if rule (LT) unevenly: tests the condition on some visits but not others (e.g. runs the branch on every loop pass without testing), runs the branch after a false test, or re-checks the condition after the branch has run. (here mixing in: "an if body repeats while its condition holds")
wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
wrong rule: Uses a loop where a condition needs to be tested only once. Right rule: A test made once is an if; a loop repeats.
wrong rule: you need an if to turn a boolean expression into a boolean. Right rule: ok = (x > y); stores the result of the comparison directly.

wrong rule: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.
wrong rule: Of two if statements one after the other, the second runs its body only if both conditions are true. Right rule: Two ifs in sequence are independent: each tests only its own condition.

Negating the condition swaps which inputs run the body; changing < to <= changes only the boundary value. Adding a statement under a braceless if does not put it in the body. Whatever the condition, code after the if still runs exactly once.
wrong rule: print and println behave the same. Right rule: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.
wrong rule: println(s) prints a newline and then s. Right rule: println(s) prints s and then the line terminator.

Applies the println rule (print, then end line) unevenly: puts the newline before the text on one call and after it on another, or forgets that the next output starts on a new line. (here mixing in: "print and println behave the same (no newline difference)")
wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names that differ only in capitalization are different names.
wrong rule: () are optional on a no-argument call like println. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.
Replacing println with print joins the next output onto the same line (a typical logic error); the characters printed stay the same.
wrong rule: The computer fills in omitted steps or values the programmer meant. Right rule: The computer executes only the statements written; every needed step and value must be written.

Applies the sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: executes the statements in order on some lines but lets a later statement's effect leak into an earlier one, or skips or repeats a statement on one pass. (here mixing in: "The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command")
wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order, so their order makes no difference. Right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom, in the order written.

wrong rule: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line. Right rule: Java compilers treat all whitespace outside quotes as equivalent; statements are separated by ;, not by line breaks.

wrong rule: The program knows what later lines will do and acts on that goal at the current line. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.
Swapping two statements that touch the same variable or the output generally changes the result; swapping independent statements, or changing only whitespace between them, keeps it.
